summary: The article surveys funding options available to retiree entrepreneurs in the local community, noting a rise in senior-founded startups since September 2023. It profiles nine financing routes, from bank loans and grants to crowdfunding, angel and venture capital, bootstrapping, CDFIs and alternative lenders, each illustrated by a local retiree's story and quote. It concludes that each option has distinct advantages and challenges, so a potential means of financing exists for every dream.
one_line: A profile of nine funding routes, each illustrated by a local retiree entrepreneur, for financing senior-founded startups since September 2023.
key_facts: Since September 2023, there has been a notable uptick in senior-founded startups across the local neighborhoods.
Maria Gonzalez, a 65-year-old former educator, opened her tutoring center in November 2023 with a modest loan from a local community bank, leveraging her good credit history.

Thomas O'Connor, a 62-year-old retired military veteran, won a government grant for service members transitioning into business ownership in January 2024; it covered equipment costs for his craft distillery concept.
Lynn Smith, aged 60, launched a successful crowdfunding campaign in October 2023 to open an art studio; she calls crowdfunding 'a pre-validation of your market.'
Crowdfunding websites named in the article are Kickstarter and Indiegogo.
George Kostas, 63, with a patent-pending invention, met an angel investor at a local business networking event in December 2023 and received a considerable investment.
Angel investors provide capital in exchange for equity.
Patricia Evans, 61, secured venture capital for her tech startup in February 2024, enabling rapid scalability; she says 'VCs bet on your future.'
Alan and Julie Chen, a couple in their sixties, bootstrapped a farm-to-table restaurant by reinvesting their life savings, which gives them complete control.
Sophia Bernard, 68, used a local Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) to start a mobile healthcare service and received both capital and guidance.
CDFIs are often non-profits that aim to empower economically disadvantaged entrepreneurs.
Jack Wallace, 64, used alternative lenders for a community radio station; their high interest rates are offset by agility and accessibility compared with banks and grant programs.
